overview: Classical Latin is the literary language of ancient Rome from approximately 100 BCE to 100 CE, the medium of Cicero, Vergil, Ovid, and Caesar. It employs a synthetic morphology with five noun declensions, four verb conjugations, and flexible word order. Mastery of Latin provides direct access to the foundational texts of Western literature, law, philosophy, and science, and illuminates the structure of the Romance languages and English vocabulary.

alphabet.name: ā
alphabet.approximation: short: 'a' in idea; long: 'a' in father
alphabet.notes: Vowel quantity (short vs. long) is phonemic and affects meter and meaning. Long vowels are marked ā in pedagogical texts.

alphabet.name: cē
alphabet.notes: Classical pronunciation is always velar [k], not the soft [s] or [tʃ] of ecclesiastical or Romance tradition.

alphabet.name: ē
alphabet.approximation: short: 'e' in pet; long: 'a' in cake (but pure, not diphthongized)

alphabet.name: hā
alphabet.notes: Pronounced in Classical Latin; often weakened or lost by the imperial period.

alphabet.name: ī
alphabet.approximation: vowel short: 'i' in bit; long: 'ee' in see; consonant: 'y' in yes
alphabet.notes: Functions as both vowel and consonant (consonantal i often written as j in modern editions). Vowel quantity is phonemic.

alphabet.name: jōta
alphabet.notes: Modern orthographic convention for consonantal i; not distinguished in classical inscriptions.

alphabet.name: kā
alphabet.notes: Rare; used only in a few words like Kalendae and Karthago.

alphabet.name: em
alphabet.notes: Final -m may have been weakly articulated or nasalized the preceding vowel in verse.

alphabet.name: ō
alphabet.approximation: short: 'o' in pot (British); long: 'o' in note (but pure)

alphabet.name: qū
alphabet.notes: Always followed by u; together qu represents the labiovelar [kʷ].

alphabet.name: er
alphabet.notes: The r was probably an alveolar trill in Classical Latin.

alphabet.name: es
alphabet.notes: Always voiceless [s], never [z] as in English 'rose'.

alphabet.name: tē
alphabet.notes: No palatalization; -ti- before vowels is [ti], not [ʃi] or [tsi] as in ecclesiastical pronunciation.

alphabet.name: ū
alphabet.approximation: vowel short: 'u' in put; long: 'oo' in moon; consonant: 'w' in water
alphabet.notes: Functions as both vowel and consonant (consonantal u often written as v in modern editions). Vowel quantity is phonemic.

alphabet.name: vē
alphabet.notes: Modern orthographic convention for consonantal u; pronounced [w], not [v]. Not distinguished from u in classical inscriptions.

alphabet.name: ȳ Graeca
alphabet.approximation: French 'u' in tu; German 'ü' in über
alphabet.notes: Used only in Greek loanwords. A front rounded vowel.

pronunciation_notes: All consonants are pronounced; no silent letters except possibly final -m in verse (nasalizes preceding vowel).
The diphthongs ae and oe are pronounced [ai̯] ('eye') and [oi̯] ('oy'), not as single vowels.
Vowel quantity (short vs. long) is phonemic and affects word stress and meaning; long vowels take approximately twice the time to pronounce.
Stress falls on the penult (second-to-last syllable) if it contains a long vowel or diphthong, or if its vowel is followed by two consonants; otherwise stress falls on the antepenult (third-to-last).
C and G are always hard ([k] and [ɡ]); consonantal I and V are semivowels ([j] and [w]), not fricatives.

grammar.noun_system: Latin nouns are declined for five cases (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative), two numbers (singular, plural), and three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter). The vocative case exists but is often identical to the nominative except in singular second-declension masculines. Case endings indicate syntactic function (subject, direct object, possession, etc.), permitting flexible word order.

declensions.name: First Declension
declensions.description: Predominantly feminine nouns with stem in -ā. Example: puella, -ae, f. 'girl'.

declensions.name: Second Declension (masculine)
declensions.description: Masculine and neuter nouns with stem in -o. Example: servus, -ī, m. 'slave, servant'.

declensions.name: Second Declension (neuter)
declensions.description: Neuter nouns in -um. Neuters have identical nominative, accusative, and vocative forms; nom./acc./voc. plural always end in -a. Example: dōnum, -ī, n. 'gift'.

declensions.name: Third Declension (consonant-stem)
declensions.description: Nouns with consonant stems; all three genders. Example: rēx, rēgis, m. 'king'.

grammar.verb_system: Latin verbs are conjugated for six tenses (present, imperfect, future, perfect, pluperfect, future perfect), three persons, two numbers, three moods (indicative, subjunctive, imperative), two voices (active, passive), and have infinite forms (infinitives, participles, gerunds, supines). The present, imperfect, and future tenses are built on the present stem; the perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect on the perfect stem.

conjugations.name: First Conjugation
conjugations.description: Verbs with present stem in -ā-. Example: amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum 'to love' (active indicative).

conjugations.name: Second Conjugation
conjugations.description: Verbs with present stem in -ē-. Example: moneō, monēre, monuī, monitum 'to warn, advise' (active indicative).

conjugations.name: Third Conjugation
conjugations.description: Verbs with consonant or short -i- stem. Example: regō, regere, rēxī, rēctum 'to rule' (active indicative).

conjugations.name: Fourth Conjugation
conjugations.description: Verbs with present stem in -ī-. Example: audiō, audīre, audīvī, audītum 'to hear' (active indicative).

terms.definition: Subject of the verb; predicate nominative. The 'who' or 'what' doing the action.
Possession or description ('of'). Shows ownership or relationship.
Indirect object ('to' or 'for'). The recipient of an action.
Direct object of the verb. The 'what' or 'whom' receiving the action.
Separation, means, accompaniment ('by', 'with', 'from'). Expresses manner, means, or place.
Direct address. Used when calling or speaking to someone.
One person or thing.
More than one person or thing.
Grammatical gender, not biological. Includes many male beings but also inanimate objects.
Grammatical gender. Includes many female beings but also inanimate objects.
Neither masculine nor feminine. Often includes things and abstract concepts.
A pattern of case endings for nouns. Latin has five declensions, each with characteristic endings.
Nouns with stem in -ā, predominantly feminine. Example: puella, -ae 'girl'.
Nouns with stem in -o, masculine and neuter. Examples: servus, -ī (m.) 'servant'; dōnum, -ī (n.) 'gift'.
Consonant-stem and i-stem nouns, all genders. Example: rēx, rēgis (m.) 'king'.
Nouns with stem in -u, mostly masculine. Example: manus, -ūs (f.) 'hand'.
Nouns with stem in -ē, mostly feminine. Example: rēs, reī (f.) 'thing'.
Action happening now or habitually. 'I love', 'I am loving'.
Ongoing or repeated action in the past. 'I was loving', 'I used to love'.
Action that will happen. 'I will love', 'I shall love'.
Completed action in the past. 'I loved', 'I have loved'.
Action completed before another past action. 'I had loved'.
Action that will be completed before a future time. 'I will have loved'.
'I' — the speaker. Example: amō 'I love'.
'You' — the person spoken to. Example: amās 'you love'.
'He/she/it' — someone/something else. Example: amat 'he/she/it loves'.
'We' — the speakers. Example: amāmus 'we love'.
'You all' — people spoken to. Example: amātis 'you (pl.) love'.
'They' — other people/things. Example: amant 'they love'.
A pattern of verb endings. Latin has four regular conjugations plus irregular verbs.
Verbs with present stem in -ā-. Example: amō, amāre 'to love'.
Verbs with present stem in -ē-. Example: moneō, monēre 'to warn'.
Verbs with consonant or short -i- stem. Example: regō, regere 'to rule'.
Verbs with present stem in -ī-. Example: audiō, audīre 'to hear'.
States facts or asks questions. The default mood for statements.
Expresses possibility, purpose, wish, or doubt. Often in subordinate clauses.
Gives commands. 'Love!' = amā (sg.), amāte (pl.).
Subject performs the action. 'I love her.'
Subject receives the action. 'I am loved by her.'

reading_list: Cicero, In Catilinam I; Pro Archia

numbers.overview: Classical Latin cardinal numbers from 1 to 3 decline fully for case, gender, and number, while 4 to 100 are mostly indeclinable adjectives. Hundreds (200, 300, etc.) and multiples of 1000 decline as plural adjectives. Ordinal numbers are regular first/second declension adjectives agreeing with their nouns in case, gender, and number.

cardinals.note: Declines as first/second declension adjective; means 'none' or 'no'
Declines like ūnus, ūna, ūnum (gen. ūnīus, dat. ūnī)
Declines irregularly: duo, duae, duo (masc., fem., neut.)
Declines: trēs, trēs, tria (masc., fem., neut.)
Indeclinable singular; plural mīlia declines as neuter i-stem
Literally 'ten times hundred thousands'; Romans had no single word

teaching_notes: Cardinals 1 to 3 decline fully. Ūnus follows the pronominal declension with genitive ūnīus and dative ūnī across all genders. Duo has separate forms for each gender (duo, duae, duo), and trēs distinguishes masculine/feminine (trēs) from neuter (tria).

Cardinals 4 through 100 are indeclinable, but hundreds (ducentī, trecentī) and thousands in the plural (mīlia) decline as adjectives or nouns. When expressing thousands, use indeclinable mīlle for 1000, but mīlia (neuter i-stem) for multiples, followed by a partitive genitive.

Numbers 18 and 19 are often expressed subtractively as duōdēvīgintī ('two from twenty') and ūndēvīgintī ('one from twenty'), though octōdecim and novemdecim also appear. The same subtractive pattern occurs with 28, 29, etc.
All ordinal numbers are regular first/second declension adjectives and must agree with their nouns in case, gender, and number. They form the basis for many Roman names (Quīntus, Sextus, Decimus).

Compound numbers are formed by writing the largest unit first, connected by et or simple juxtaposition: vīgintī ūnus (21), centum et ūnus (101). The smaller number can decline if it is 1 to 3: cum duōbus et vīgintī mīlitibus ('with twenty-two soldiers').
